author: James Brumley
title: Every three months I take an exploratory look how smartphone
text:
Every three months I take an exploratory look how smartphone market share is changing. And every three months I take something of a verbal beating for suggesting that Apple ( AAPL ) might not have the stranglehold on that market that its fans and followers might like to think it has.
Apparently I’m a glutton, because I’m getting ready to do it again. Gartner’s recent look at the fourth quarter’s smartphone sales data once again hints that the iPhone – though it never owned a majority of the market – is slipping.
And once again, it matters not because Apple is still the only company making any real profits in the smartphone game, but because usage of differing operating systems is the key to this market’s future.
What I’m Not Saying In the past I’ve started with a look at the raw numbers and then offered up my interpretation of what the data means… a mistake, in that most readers don’t bother reading the analysis. So, just to make clear from the onset what I’m not saying, a failure to win smartphone market share in and of itself isn’t the same as a grim outlook. Apple on its worst day is still a better investment than most other companies on their worst days.
And I’ll also say it before anyone else does: Apple is the only smartphone maker making any real money by being in the smartphone-sales business. Though they’re only estimates, TechInsights believes Apple is clearing more than $600 for each of the smaller iPhone Xs it sells, while the iPhone 8 translates into a per-unit profit of around $400.
That’s impressive.
But, that’s also not the point. The key takeaway here is, in that the big growth engine in the smartphone business isn’t hardware but the operating system as an app-sales and advertising platform, Apple isn’t firing on all cylinders. Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ), which of course makes the far more ubiquitous Android operating system, is slowly but surely positioning itself to win the next era of the war.
In that light, even the staunchest of Apple investors would be wise to give this idea - and the supporting data - some thought.
Losing Market Share The data speaks for itself. According to Gartner, during the final quarter of 2016, Apple sold 77.0 million iPhones. During the fourth quarter of 2017, it only sold 73.2 million units .
Source: Gartner, table made by author 
Perhaps more meaningful, Apple’s market share remained level, at 17.9%. Samsung’s ( OTC:SSNLF ) advanced from 17.8% a year ago to 18.2% for the final quarter of 2017, despite a notable drop-off in the number of smartphone sold that adversely impacted all manufacturers. The big winners, surprisingly enough, were Huawei and Xiaomi (Private: XI ) , catering to the lower-end of the smartphone market with entry-level priced devices.
Source: Gartner, table made by author 
The knee-jerk reaction from at least some observers: Higher-priced iPhones crimped total sales , but didn’t crimp total revenue last quarter. The success Huawei and Oppo and Xiaomi have been creating of late is a sliver of the market Apple was never aiming at anyway.
I wholeheartedly agree. And kudos to Apple for its most profitable quarter ever . As was noted already though, that’s not the point or purpose of this look. In focus here is what shrinking usage of the iOS operating system may ultimately mean in an environment where smartphone saturation is a real thing ( part of the reason the smartphone market shrank last quarter), and when at least more than a few consumers are starting to question the need for a phone that costs four figures.
It’s a small headwind now. All big trends start out as small ones though.
The picture worsens, by the way, when you zoom out to the full-year data. Apple was the only recognizable name in the smartphone business to ship fewer smartphones in 2017 than it did in 2016, letting its market share slide from 14.4% to 14% on a full-year basis… the only name to earn that dubious honor.
Source: Gartner, table made by author
Where it Hurts the Most The bigger red flag buried in the data is the fact that iOS also lost market share in 2017.
Source: Gartner, table made by author 
And let’s not pretend like iOS as a sales tool isn’t important. The company’s “Services” revenue was up 18% year-over-year last quarter , making it the second-biggest arm now. At $8.5 billion in revenue for Q4, though it still pales in comparison to the $61.6 billion worth of iPhones Apple sold during the quarter, it’s still a bigger business than iPads or Mac computers.
Its apps and digital media arm also has been the most-touted growth driver of late, by the company and its supporters.
Bottom Line Just to head off the counterarguments at the proverbial pass, this doesn’t even remotely suggest that Apple is facing inevitable ruin. Apple is going to be fine. And it’s absolutely true that Apple earns the bulk of the smartphone industry’s profits.
The data above, however, also points to the reality that the premium smartphone market is near or at the point of saturation, and has largely been split between Samsung and Apple. Any net growth in the number of smartphone owners the world sees is likely already spoken for by the lower-cost suppliers.
That’s the long way of saying it’s time for Apple to reinvent itself if it wants to keep growing the way it has in the past - ever-increasing phone prices aren’t a long-term solution. It’s not clear, though, that sort of marketable innovation is being done (and there’s certainly not the kind of innovation we saw in 2007, when the company made iPhones a more important growth tool than computers in the works).
Services, or the sale of more apps and more digital media? That certainly looks like the go-to revenue source, but that business is still less than one-fifth the size of Apple’s iPhone business. There’s a lot of growing to be done if that’s the next lever Tim Cook is going to pull in a big way and keep driving the growth investors have grown accustomed to.
The risk in looking through the above lens is assuming this paradigm shift has to be done and perfected by next week. It doesn’t. Apple could arguably coast another couple of years as lingering, aspirational smartphone fans finally take the plunge on the "next" iPhone. That will give the company time to figure out how to sell more digital music, videos and apps.
On the other hand, it would be naive to believe this bigger-picture change isn’t happening. Apple has to adapt, and it will. It’s just not clear how successful that adaptation is going to be.
